findings.description: The check still does not detect this clause's second stated failing example. Revision 2 moved the TAP requirement into the clause text — "The script parses `bats --formatter tap` output and confirms the mutated case itself reports `not ok`" — but gave the check no way to verify the text was followed. Walk the three parts against failing example 2 ("one that mutates every site correctly but concludes from the file's exit status alone, so a mutation that introduces a syntax error counts as a success while the assertion it was probing was never evaluated"): part 1, a script with a correct `assert_contains`/`assert_not_contains` form parser and an exit-status success criterion mutates all 53 and exits 0 — passes. Part 2, its per-file counts are exactly right — passes. Part 3, `true` matches no recognised form, so its parser errors and it exits non-zero — passes. All three parts green against the artifact the clause says must fail. This is the same shape as revision 1's blockers: the requirement is stated, the check cannot see it. A deterministic probe does exist and discriminates cleanly — in the scratch worktree plant a failure unrelated to any mutation (an unterminated `@test` is enough), re-run, and require the script to report that file's sites as un-reddened and exit non-zero. An exit-status script counts them all as successes; a TAP script sees the named case never reported `not ok`.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:239-244 (the three parts and the failing example) against constitution.md:236 (the text the parts do not verify). Reproduced: a two-case bats file loading helpers, with an unterminated `@test` appended and `assert_contains "hello"` inverted to `assert_not_contains "hello"` -> bats prints `not ok 1 setup_file failed`, `bats warning: Executed 1 instead of expected 2 tests`, and the file exits 1. The mutated case (`case A`) never appears in TAP output at all, so file exit status reports a success that per-case TAP correctly reports as a non-result.

findings.description: The clause's account of its own reach is false in both directions, and the hole it names is now owned by no one. V-2 opens "A conversion that always passes is the same bug wearing better syntax, and nothing else in this constitution would catch it: B-1 sees a converted line, B-2 sees a plausible needle, V-3 sees a green suite." Measured against revision 2's own fixed mutation rule, V-2 is the clause that cannot catch it: an always-true assertion inverts to an always-false one, which reddens, so the mutation reports success. That is not a defect in the rule — polarity inversion cannot distinguish a tautology from a live assertion by construction, and rejecting my revision 1 tautology probe was correct. The defect is the sentence. B-2's rubric does carry the FAIL condition ("replaces a condition with one that cannot fail"), so the constitution as a whole still covers this — but V-2's text tells its reader that B-2 will not, and B-2's checker is never told it is the sole line of defence on the job's central failure mode. V-2 should say it proves an assertion is *wired in*, not that it is *meaningful*, and hand meaningfulness to B-2 by name.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:224 against constitution.md:230 and constitution.md:168. Measured with the repo's own helper bodies: a case containing `assert_contains ""` reports `ok` (grep with an empty pattern matches every line), and the same case with V-2's mutation applied — `assert_not_contains ""` — reports `not ok`, because `case "$h" in *""*` matches everything. So a site converted to an empty needle passes B-1, passes B-3, keeps V-3 green, and passes V-2's mutation pass cleanly.

findings.description: The new grep hardening declares the passing case `blocked`, and it fires on every correct run. `grep -c` exits 1 whenever the count is 0 — that is the no-match case, not an error — so the specified pipeline on a clean tree prints `0` and exits 1. The clause then says "a non-zero exit from `grep` itself is `blocked`, not a pass." A checker-deterministic following the letter reports `blocked` on exactly the outcome the clause is asking for, which under the guild contract means fix-the-check-and-re-dispatch: a loop that only the orchestrator can break. B-1's parallel sentence gets this right by naming exit 2 specifically, and so does the global note on `grep` ("exit 1 means no match and exit 2 means the check failed to run") — which V-3 cites by name in the same sentence it contradicts.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:254 against constitution.md:39 and constitution.md:151. Measured at 61213fe on a clean tree: `git diff 61213fe..HEAD -- tests/ | /usr/bin/grep -cE '^\+[[:space:]]*skip\b'` -> prints `0`, exit 1. Same pattern against a line that does match -> prints `1`, exit 0.

findings.description: The mutation harness assumes the work is already committed, and the previous job's `cp` lesson did not come across with the rest of the fix. `git worktree add /tmp/agc-lint HEAD` gives a tree at HEAD. If V-1's checker runs before D-3's commit — and nothing in the constitution orders them — then `tests/lint.bats`, `tests/helpers.bash`, and `tests/mutation-check.sh` do not exist in that worktree at all: `bats tests/lint.bats` errors instead of reporting `not ok`, planting 2 and 3 create untracked files rather than appending to real ones, and `git checkout tests/helpers.bash` fails on a path git does not know. A correct worker gets FAILed by a check that never ran. The archive constitution wrote this down explicitly for exactly this reason ("note the `cp`, without which the worktree carries HEAD's unmodified doctor.bats and the step is inert"). One sentence closes it: run this after the work is committed, or `cp` the three files into the worktree first and restore by re-copying rather than by `git checkout`.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:196-215 against archive/2026-08-07/constitution.md:211-219 (`git worktree add /tmp/agc-mut HEAD` followed by `cp tests/doctor.bats /tmp/agc-mut/tests/`) and archive/2026-08-07/constitution.md:177-181. At 61213fe, `ls tests/` returns seven `.bats` files and nothing else, so all three planting targets are files this job creates.

findings.description: The helper-call count is off by one, in the clause that now owns the helper-call contract. 54 sites = 53 assertions + `tests/packages.bats:146`, per the Measured baseline's own "53 assertions, plus one that is not." Of the 53 assertions, `doctor.bats:244` becomes an `if` rather than a helper call, so **52** call helpers, not 51. No reading reconciles the clause's sentence: taking "these two" as the two exceptions, 51 + 2 = 53 only if `packages.bats:146` is counted among the assertions, which contradicts the baseline; and 51 + 2 = 53 leaves the 54 sites one short. A checker redoing this arithmetic — which is the natural way to check "every containment assertion calls a shared helper" — will land on 52 and have to ask which number governs.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:167 (`That leaves 51 helper calls, plus these two, plus doctor.bats:244 counted among the 53 assertions V-2 mutates`) against constitution.md:97 (the table: 54 sites, 53 assertions), constitution.md:110, and constitution.md:164-165 (the two exceptions). Re-derived at 61213fe: 54 first-token sites; `tests/packages.bats` holds 4 sites of which :117, :119, :120 are assertions and :146 is the `|| continue` guard, confirming the table's packages column of 3.

findings.description: The heredoc paragraph mandates work against a set that is empty at baseline, without saying so. "Converting or rewording those is in scope" reads as though there are heredoc-enclosed sites to convert; a heredoc-aware scan of all seven files finds none — every one of the 54 sites is ordinary test-body code. The rule itself is right and worth keeping as a forward constraint on stub bodies a worker writes during conversion; it just needs "there are none at baseline" attached, so a worker does not hunt for them and a checker does not expect them in the diff.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:144. Measured at 61213fe with a heredoc-tracking scan across tests/*.bats (tracking `<<`/`<<-` delimiters and their terminators): zero of the 54 first-token sites falls inside a heredoc body. Ten heredoc stub writes exist (tests/apps.bats:30, :39; tests/doctor.bats:30, :260; tests/font.bats:31, :42; tests/install-failures.bats:52, :99, :211, :271, :342; tests/licensed-fonts.bats:31), none containing a first-token `[[`.

findings.description: Pinning `doctor.bats:244` by line number inside a script the clause calls "committed and reusable" makes the script silently wrong after any later edit above that line in `doctor.bats`. The failure direction is safe — a stale pointer means the site stops matching a recognised form, which the clause already turns into a hard error — so this costs a confusing failure rather than a false pass. Anchoring on the case title or on the two needles would survive the next edit.

At 61213fe the site is tests/doctor.bats:244, `[[ "$output" == *"undeclared"* || "$output" == *"casks"* ]]`, the last statement of its case; B-3's mandated `load` line alone moves it to :245.

findings.description: Part 1's definition grep is keyed to one spelling of a function definition. `^[[:space:]]*(assert_contains|assert_not_contains)[[:space:]]*\(\)` requires the `name() {` form on a single line; `function assert_contains() {` or a definition whose parens sit on a following line returns fewer than 2 and fails a perfectly good `helpers.bash`. Low risk, because the repo idiom already matches — `tests/install-failures.bats:73` and `:78` are both `name() {` — but the check is stricter than the requirement it stands for.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:178. tests/install-failures.bats:73 is `assert_contains() {` and :78 is `assert_not_contains() {`, both matching; the requirement in the clause text is only that helpers.bash "defines at minimum assert_contains and assert_not_contains".

findings.description: Correcting my own revision 1 finding: the orchestrator is right, and my claim was overstated. Re-ran the identical BRE form five times this session — `printf '+\tskip foo\n' | grep '^\+\s*skip\b'` — and it matched with exit 0 every time, same as `/usr/bin/grep`, and the `-cE` form the orchestrator tried matched too. The shim is real and still installed, and I did observe the compile error twice in the revision 1 session, so the hazard class is genuine; but it is intermittent and I could not reproduce it on demand, so it should be recorded as a precaution taken rather than a defect measured. Keep the hardening — `/usr/bin/grep` with POSIX classes costs nothing and removes a variable — but the r0 finding as I wrote it asserted more than I can now re-derive, and the constitution should not cite it as a measured failure.
findings.evidence: Measured this session: `printf '+\tskip foo\n' | grep '^\+\s*skip\b'` -> matches, exit 0, five trials. `printf '+\tskip foo\n' | grep -cE '^\+\s*skip\b'` -> prints 1, exit 0. `grep --version` -> `ugrep 7.5.0`, so the shim is still in place. Against the revision 1 session, where the same BRE form returned `ugrep: error: error at position 5 ... invalid syntax`, exit 2, twice.

findings.description: Blocker 1 is genuinely closed. The clause's failing example is "a guard case that scans only `tests/*.bats` and never `tests/helpers.bash`", and planting 2 now appends a `canary()` containing a first-token `[[` to `tests/helpers.bash` and requires `not ok` on its own. A `.bats`-only guard cannot see that planting, reports `ok`, and fails the check — so the check now catches the artifact its failing example describes, which is precisely what revision 1 could not do. Planting 3 extends the same logic to `mutation-check.sh`, and the `BATS_TEST_DIRNAME` requirement from my r0 minor is in the clause text.

findings.description: Blocker 4 is closed, and putting `mutation-check.sh` on the surface introduced no contradiction I can find. The surface is now stated once, normatively, in B-1, with an explicit prohibition on any other clause restating it; V-1 and B-3 both cite it by reference and neither narrows it. Checked the side effects the change was most likely to have: the script needs the helper names as literal strings but never needs a first-token `[[`, so the rule is satisfiable; `tests/lint.bats` needs the pattern and B-1 says outright that the first-token rule is what keeps it from flagging itself; `bats tests/` collects only `*.bats`, so a shell script under `tests/` is never executed by V-3; `tests/` is inside D-1's allowlist, so the new file is in scope. Nothing on the surface is required by one clause and exempted by another. The exit-2-is-blocked handling closes my r0 minor about a missing `helpers.bash` reading as clean.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:136-153 against constitution.md:188 (V-1: `which B-1 defines and this clause does not restate`), constitution.md:176 (B-3 cites the surface), constitution.md:262 (D-1 allows tests/). Verified `bash` on this host resolves to /bin/bash 3.2.57(1)-release and there is no second bash on PATH, so B-1's stated rationale that `mutation-check.sh` runs under the same 3.2 holds for the invocation V-2 specifies.

findings.description: Blocker 3's requirement landed correctly in the clause text, and the reasoning behind it is stated well enough that a future revision will not undo it: "a mutation that breaks bash parsing, or that trips some other case in the same file, produces a non-zero exit while the mutated case never failed. That is the reasoning this clause's own failing example condemns, and revision 1 committed it." The gap is only that the check cannot verify compliance — the blocker above. Separately, the mutation rule is now genuinely fixed rather than left to the worker: helper-name swap for polarity, sentinel needles for the disjunction, and an unrecognised form as a hard error rather than a silent skip. That last one is the right call and is what makes part 3 decidable where revision 1's tautology probe was not.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:226-236. The `true` probe is decidable as claimed: `true` is not `assert_contains` or `assert_not_contains` and is not the named disjunction site, so any script with a real form parser must reach its unrecognised-form branch.

The helper-call requirement is stated as a rule rather than an aspiration, with the reason a syntax-only ban is insufficient spelled out ("Forbidding `[[` alone would be satisfied by inlining a bare `grep -qF` at all 53 sites"), and `tests/packages.bats:146`'s required form moved out of descriptive prose into the clause, with an explicit FAIL for deleting it and a second failing example illustrating the deletion path. The Measured baseline now defers to B-2 on that form rather than restating it, which is the right direction of dependency.
